claims.text: Annealing just below the bulk phase-coarsening temperature can induce an interfacial complexion at lamellar-colony boundaries.
The induced interfacial complexion will be thin.
The induced interfacial complexion will be coherent and ductile.
The interfacial complexion will reduce local stress concentrations at lamellar-colony boundaries.
Reducing boundary stress concentrations will mitigate microcrack nucleation.
Interfacial modification can occur without altering the bulk FCC/B2 phase morphology.
The treated alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified baseline.
The treated alloy will maintain or enhance room-temperature tensile strength relative to the unmodified baseline.
The intervention can simultaneously improve room-temperature tensile strength and ductility.
The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has an FCC/B2 dual-phase microstructure.
The initial FCC/B2 microstructure consists of lamellar colonies produced by conventional processing.
The conventional microstructure contains numerous internal colony boundaries.
Microcracks typically nucleate at the internal boundaries during room-temperature tensile deformation.
The conventional baseline has high strength at the expense of tensile ductility.
The baseline's limited ductility is caused by microcrack initiation at unmodified internal boundaries.
Temperature and duration must be controlled to prevent bulk phase coarsening or unwanted transformations.
The intervention will be effective only when it modifies interfaces without changing the overall lamellar structure.
The stability of the proposed complexion and the magnitude and parameter sensitivity of the mechanical-property changes are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis asserts improvement in both strength and ductility, but the predicted outcome permits strength merely to be maintained, whereas the falsification rule requires statistically significant improvement in both properties.
